cards.title: Ten signup-form mistakes to audit before scaling list growth
cards.summary: Diagnostic checklist of the ten most common popup failures, from weak offers and too many fields to slow images and codes given away too early.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing store popup that gets traffic but converts poorly.

cards.title: A/B test the offer holistically, not by signup rate alone
cards.summary: When split testing signup incentives, judge by welcome-flow placed-order rate, AOV and attributed revenue together, not the form's submit rate.
cards.use_when: Deciding which popup incentive (percentage off, dollar off, BOGO, gift, free shipping, mystery discount) the store should run.

cards.title: Add a micro-yes step before the email field
cards.summary: A prior 'Do you want 10% off?' commitment step can lift submit rates by getting an initial yes, but the source reports it works better for some brands without it.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the capture popup's form structure with an extra qualifying step.

cards.title: Reap the main email lifecycle payoff: LTV and AOV, not only last-click revenue
cards.summary: Email's core value is raising customer lifetime value and average order value and reducing reliance on paid ads, not just collecting one-off email revenue.
cards.use_when: Planning the email channel's role in the store's overall acquisition and retention mix, and justifying budget and effort.

cards.title: Micro-yes signup step: ask for consent before email capture
cards.summary: Inserting a 'Do you want 10% off?' micro-commitment step before the email field can lift signup conversion, but must be split-tested per brand.
cards.use_when: Designing or A/B testing the newsletter/SMS signup form (popup or full page) for an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Signup form tests: delay, format, and audience size
cards.summary: Test popup delay, popup vs full page, and other form variables on total signups, not just signup rate.
cards.use_when: Optimizing the newsletter signup popup for an ecommerce store, deciding timing and format.

cards.title: Visual signup form tests: color, images, and imagery content
cards.summary: Test plain vs designed, light vs dark, contrasting fields, and image presence/content on the signup form.
cards.use_when: Designing the visual layout of an ecommerce newsletter popup or signup page.

cards.title: SMS opt-in angles after email signup
cards.summary: Test offer-equivalence vs upgraded offer vs VIP-club angle for the SMS opt-in step.
cards.use_when: Adding or optimizing an SMS list opt-in step within the email signup flow.

cards.title: Flow structure and profile filters in Klaviyo
cards.summary: Understand flow triggers, profile filters (order/cart/checkout exclusions), and profile properties to prevent overlapping emails.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing Klaviyo flows for an ecommerce store so customers don't receive conflicting sequences.

cards.title: Use past profiles to backfill newly launched flows
cards.summary: Backfill a new flow so eligible customers enter at the correct stage instead of waiting for the delay to elapse.
cards.use_when: Launching a winback, re-engagement, or time-delayed flow and wanting it to act on past behavior immediately.

cards.title: Turn off smart sending for flows, keep it on for campaigns
cards.summary: Disable smart sending in flows so abandoned-cart/checkout emails aren't skipped; keep it enabled for campaigns.
cards.use_when: Configuring send settings inside any Klaviyo flow email for an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Welcome series structure: 7 emails with distinct angles
cards.summary: Build a welcome series that delivers the incentive fast, then rotates through brand story, bestsellers, reviews, USP comparison, and expiring-discount urgency.
cards.use_when: Building or rewriting the welcome flow for an ecommerce store after newsletter signup.

cards.title: Site abandonment flow: trigger, delay, and one guiding email
cards.summary: Build a site-abandonment flow for visitors who never viewed a product, using the active-on-site trigger and a 1–4 hour delay.
cards.use_when: Recovering early-stage site visitors (homepage/blog visitors who did not view a product) for an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Browse abandonment flow: trigger, filters, and review-led emails
cards.summary: Set up a browse-abandonment flow triggered by viewed product, with product-specific reviews and a discount only after several emails.
cards.use_when: Re-engaging shoppers who viewed a product but never added to cart on an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Abandoned cart flow: trigger distinction and 6–8 email structure
cards.summary: Build a true added-to-cart abandonment flow (not the mislabeled checkout default) with a 30-minute-to-2-hour delay and staged email angles.
cards.use_when: Setting up or fixing the abandoned cart sequence for an ecommerce store in Klaviyo.

cards.title: Checkout abandonment flow: same structure, different objections
cards.summary: Clone the abandoned cart flow and retarget checkout starters with content tailored to late-stage objections like shipping costs.
cards.use_when: Recovering shoppers who started checkout but did not complete the purchase on an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Time-delay heuristics by journey stage
cards.summary: First-email delays should shorten as the customer moves from browsing to checkout, and each delay should be split-tested.
cards.use_when: Setting or tuning the first-email delay inside ecommerce abandonment flows.

cards.title: Subject line, preview text, and sender name optimization
cards.summary: Treat preview text as a second subject line, test sender names, and keep sender email consistent across all sends.
cards.use_when: Configuring email metadata for ecommerce flows and campaigns in Klaviyo.

cards.title: Bulk flow action status and flow analytics
cards.summary: Use flow-level settings to publish/draft all emails at once and analyze flow performance over custom time frames.
cards.use_when: Managing, launching, or reviewing ecommerce email flows in Klaviyo.

cards.title: Decide whether to use Klaviyo's default flow templates
cards.summary: Klaviyo's prebuilt templates are a starting point for beginners, but custom-built flows typically convert better.
cards.use_when: Choosing whether to start an ecommerce flow from a Klaviyo template or build from scratch.

cards.title: Exclude engaged customers from overlapping flows
cards.summary: Use profile filters so customers advance to the next journey stage without receiving overlapping flows.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing ecommerce email flow logic to prevent a customer receiving conflicting or repetitive sequences.

cards.title: Use trigger filters for product- and collection-specific flows
cards.summary: Trigger filters let you limit browse/cart abandonment flows to specific products or collections for more relevant messaging.
cards.use_when: Building product-specific or collection-specific abandonment sequences in Klaviyo for an ecommerce catalog.

cards.title: Use plain-text founder emails and real urgency for final conversion
cards.summary: End long flows with a plain-text founder email that carries real, verifiable urgency rather than a designed template.
cards.use_when: Writing the final emails of ecommerce welcome, cart, checkout, or browse sequences to convert holdouts.

cards.title: Clone the Core Pre-Purchase Flows Instead of Building from Scratch
cards.summary: Build the five essential pre-purchase flows (welcome, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon) by cloning one proven template and swapping the trigger and one filter.
cards.use_when: Standing up pre-purchase automation for a store from zero, or when you need to ship cart/checkout abandonment emails quickly without redesigning content for each.

cards.title: Add a Cancelled-Order Filter to Post-Purchase Flows
cards.summary: Protect post-purchase flows from sending to people who cancelled their order by adding a 'cancelled order zero times' profile filter at the trigger.
cards.use_when: Setting up a post-purchase or customer thank-you flow, where someone could place an order and then cancel before the flow finishes sending.

cards.title: Time Your First Post-Purchase Email Around Transactional Emails
cards.summary: Delay the first post-purchase email ~30 minutes instead of sending instantly, because the transactional order-confirmation email already fires immediately.
cards.use_when: Designing the first email in a post-purchase/customer thank-you flow, deciding the initial send delay.

cards.title: Split Post-Purchase Email 1 by First-Time vs Returning Buyer, Then Merge Paths
cards.summary: Branch the first post-purchase email on order count to give first-time and returning buyers different thank-you copy, then recombine into one path for the rest of the flow.
cards.use_when: Building the branching logic of a post-purchase flow and deciding which portions should be segmented.

cards.title: Use the First Post-Purchase Email to Reduce Buyer's Remorse and Cross-Sell Softly
cards.summary: Send a plain-text founder/team thank-you email that builds trust after payment and adds a low-pressure 'add to your order' cross-sell line.
cards.use_when: Writing the first post-purchase email content, especially for the 24–48 hours after purchase when doubt peaks.

cards.title: Sequence the Post-Purchase Flow Around Shipping, Usage, Loyalty, Reviews and Cross-Sell
cards.summary: Structure the post-purchase flow as: thank-you (30 min) → excitement/usage guide (~2 days) → loyalty intro (~10 days) → review request (+3 days) → cross-sell with deadline emails.
cards.use_when: Mapping the full email sequence and delays of a post-purchase flow for a physical product.

cards.title: Target the First-to-Second Purchase Gap as the Hardest Retention Step
cards.summary: Prioritize converting a first-time buyer into a second-time buyer, since the source says this is the most difficult transition, versus repeat-buyer reorders which come more easily.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to invest retention/win-back effort — loyalty, post-purchase, and win-back flows — and setting expectations for which cohort to focus on.

cards.title: Set Win-Back Timing from Your Own Buying Cycle Data
cards.summary: Trigger a customer win-back flow off a purchase plus a wait equal to your brand's typical repurchase cycle, then verify the delay against your Shopify data and A/B test it.
cards.use_when: Configuring the trigger and delay for a customer win-back flow for lapsed customers.

cards.title: Escalate Win-Back Offers Slowly with Long Delays to Avoid Annoying Lapsed Customers
cards.summary: In a win-back flow, start non-discounted, introduce a discount only after two emails, then escalate, using longer delays between emails since lapsed subscribers are less engaged.
cards.use_when: Writing the email sequence and offer cadence for a customer win-back flow.

cards.title: Run a Sunset Flow to Re-Engage or Suppress Unengaged Subscribers
cards.summary: Send a plain-text sunset flow to unengaged subscribers whose only goal is an open (re-engagement), and update a profile property to suppress those who never open.
cards.use_when: Cleaning your list and protecting deliverability by identifying and suppressing subscribers who haven't engaged in a long window (e.g., 90–120+ days).

cards.title: Have the Five Core Flows Plus Win-Back and Sunset in Place
cards.summary: Prioritize the essential lifecycle flows the source calls the biggest money-makers: welcome series, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase, win-back, and sunset.
cards.use_when: Auditing which automation flows a store still needs, or sequencing which flows to build first.

cards.title: Turn Smart Sending Off for Flows, On for Campaigns
cards.summary: Disable smart sending in flows so intended emails always send, but keep it enabled in campaigns ~99.9% of the time; enable UTM tracking on campaigns.
cards.use_when: Configuring flow and campaign send settings to control when emails are skipped versus always delivered.

cards.title: Choose Among Drag-and-Drop, Plain Text, or HTML Email Editors
cards.summary: Prefer the drag-and-drop editor for most marketing emails, use plain text for personal/deliverability-sensitive sends, and avoid raw HTML due to rendering issues.
cards.use_when: Deciding which email editor to use when building a campaign or flow email.

cards.title: Use Seven Campaign Buckets to Source Email Ideas
cards.summary: Classify every campaign idea into one of seven buckets — promos, holidays/events, product launches, product highlights, social proof, value-based, and company updates — to keep your calendar varied.
cards.use_when: Generating campaign ideas and building a varied campaign calendar that doesn't fatigue your list.

cards.title: Cap Discount Frequency with a 5:1 to 10:1 Non-Discount Ratio
cards.summary: Keep at least a 5:1 ratio of non-discounted to discounted emails (the source prefers 10:1 and a max of one discount email per month) to protect brand perception and long-term results.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign cadence and deciding how often to deploy discounts across your email calendar.

cards.title: Set Campaign Frequency from Revenue Tier, Then Adjust by Metrics
cards.summary: Use rough revenue tiers (under 50k → 2–3/week; over 50k → 3–4/week; over 200k → 4–5/week) as a starting point, then adjust based on open and unsubscribe rates, never going above ~5/week.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many campaigns per week to send, and whether to scale frequency up or pull back.

cards.title: Plan the Campaign Calendar by Layering Events, Value Content, and Company News
cards.summary: Build a monthly campaign calendar in four steps: list relevant holidays/events, pick value-based content, add company events, then fill gaps with the remaining buckets — keeping a varied mix.
cards.use_when: Building out a month's campaign schedule and filling empty send slots with a non-repetitive mix.

cards.title: Run Campaign Calendar Planning in a Shared Planning Tool
cards.summary: Track your email calendar consistently in a shared tool (Airtable, Notion, ClickUp, Monday, or a Google Sheet) so everyone involved sees the same plan.
cards.use_when: Setting up the operational workflow and documentation for planning and shipping campaigns.

cards.title: Design Emails for Conversion, Not Just Aesthetics — Favor Simplicity
cards.summary: Treat email design as a conversion mechanism: use simple, digestible layouts with a clear value proposition, no blobs of text, and no excessive colors or callouts.
cards.use_when: Designing campaign and flow emails, especially deciding how much copy and visual decoration to include.

cards.title: Use Visual Hierarchies (Z, Inverted Triangle, F Patterns) to Guide the Eye to the CTA
cards.summary: Arrange email elements along familiar eye-movement patterns — zigzag/Z, inverted triangle, or F — so the reader flows naturally toward the main CTA button.
cards.use_when: Laying out an email's sections and deciding where to place headlines, body copy, images, and the CTA button.

cards.title: Replace Long Paragraphs with Visual Formats (Checklists, Tables, Comparisons)
cards.summary: Swap text-heavy explanations for visuals like checklists, comparison tables, and graphs, which are easier to digest and reduce friction.
cards.use_when: Writing email body copy that would otherwise become a long paragraph, especially product comparisons or multi-point explanations.

cards.title: Treat the Above-the-Fold Section as Decisive — Include Headline, Support, and CTA
cards.summary: Optimize the visible-without-scrolling section with an attention-grabbing headline, supporting image/text, and a call to action button, since most readers decide whether to continue from it.
cards.use_when: Designing the top of any email — campaign or flow — where you choose what appears before the reader scrolls.

cards.title: Build a Modular Figma Email Template Library for Fast, Varied Design
cards.summary: Maintain a Figma library of interchangeable section templates (headers, product sections, body sections, review blocks) so email design starts from building blocks rather than a blank canvas.
cards.use_when: Setting up an email design system, especially when producing many emails or serving multiple brands and needing variation.

cards.title: Slice a Figma email into image sections before importing to Klaviyo
cards.summary: Cut a designed email into separate exported images so each block loads fast and can carry its own product link.
cards.use_when: Importing a Figma-designed campaign into Klaviyo or another ESP, or diagnosing slow/clipped campaign emails.

cards.title: Set alt text, deep links and auto-applied discount codes on email images
cards.summary: Every email image needs descriptive alt text and a deep link, ideally with the discount code embedded so it applies automatically at checkout.
cards.use_when: Building or QAing a campaign in an ESP, specifically linking product images and setting alt attributes.

cards.title: Size, pad and fix email images so they render correctly on mobile
cards.summary: Import images with generous padding and toggle full-width text on mobile to avoid awkward desktop padding on small screens.
cards.use_when: Finalizing email layout in an ESP drag-and-drop builder and checking the mobile preview.

cards.title: Cap products per campaign email at three to four and keep the offer above the fold
cards.summary: Limit product blocks in a campaign and make offer, code and CTA visible without scrolling to protect both deliverability and choice.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing a promotional campaign's layout and product selection.

cards.title: Build reusable universal blocks for footer and repeated email sections
cards.summary: Save recurring email sections as ESP universal blocks so one edit updates every campaign that includes them.
cards.use_when: Setting up an ESP template system or updating a footer/category block across past and future campaigns.

cards.title: Use the four segmentation types to decide what to build first
cards.summary: Choose segment logic from behavioral, demographic, engagement-level and purchase-history dimensions before building in the ESP.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's segmentation structure or assigning messages to different customer groups.

cards.title: Build engaged segments across 30/60/90/120-day windows including website activity
cards.summary: Create cloneable engaged segments that blend order, checkout, cart, product-view and site-activity signals, then clone for each time window.
cards.use_when: Deciding who receives regular campaigns, or building the audience logic for retention and reactivation.

cards.title: Build buyer, non-buyer and repeat-buyer segments for tailored messaging
cards.summary: Segment buyers by purchase count and separate non-buyers, since a first-time buyer and a five-time buyer need different treatment.
cards.use_when: Planning campaigns and flows that treat new, repeat and never-purchased customers differently.

cards.title: Build abandonment and window-shopper segments for targeted recovery campaigns
cards.summary: Segment people who started checkout or added to cart but didn't buy, and high-intent browsers who never purchased.
cards.use_when: Designing cart/checkout abandonment campaigns and browser-targeting flows.

cards.title: Define VIP segments by purchase count or spend relative to AOV
cards.summary: Combine a repeat-purchase threshold with a spend threshold around four times AOV to identify VIPs, tuned to your brand.
cards.use_when: Setting up loyalty or VIP targeting, or deciding which customers get premium treatment.

cards.title: Build unengaged segments, then suppress or exclude them
cards.summary: Identify recipients with no opens, clicks, orders or site activity plus enough received emails, then suppress them or send a sunset flow.
cards.use_when: List hygiene, deliverability protection and building a sunset/re-engagement flow.

cards.title: Create bounced-email and spam-complaint segments and exclude them by default
cards.summary: Segment hard and soft bounces and spam complaints separately, suppress hard bounces immediately and exclude all three from every campaign.
cards.use_when: Protecting sender reputation and cleaning your sending list in the ESP.

cards.title: Split subject line and preview text to stay readable on mobile
cards.summary: Short subject lines plus a complementary preview text raise the chance the whole first impression is read on a small screen.
cards.use_when: Writing campaign subject lines and preheaders for a store's promotions or content sends.

cards.title: Write email headlines as outcomes, not features
cards.summary: Headlines in the header section should sell the reader's benefit or outcome rather than product specifications.
cards.use_when: Writing the hero/header copy for a product or promotional campaign email.

cards.title: Apply reading-level, brevity and one-message rules to email body copy
cards.summary: Body copy should read at roughly a fifth-grade level, cut 20–30% of words, focus on one thing, and flow sentence to sentence.
cards.use_when: Drafting or editing campaign body copy and product-block descriptions.

cards.title: Do audience research before writing, and use copy frameworks as invisible scaffolding
cards.summary: Spend most of the copywriting effort on understanding the audience; let frameworks like AIDA or PAS shape copy without forcing the structure.
cards.use_when: Preparing to write a campaign or flow sequence for a specific customer group.

cards.title: Cut copy: easy words, active voice, no fluff
cards.summary: Final-pass editing removes adverbs, passive voice, alliteration and complexity so copy reads fast and sounds human.
cards.use_when: Final editing pass on campaign copy, PDP copy or ad copy before scheduling.

cards.title: Prioritize A/B tests by recipient volume, not by ease
cards.summary: Focus split tests on the emails and flows in your account that reach the most recipients so any win compounds across revenue.
cards.use_when: Deciding which email or flow to test next when you can only run a limited number of experiments per month on your store's lifecycle program.

cards.title: Test send time against place order rate, not open rate
cards.summary: Run send-time split tests with place order rate as the winning metric because the hour with the best open rate is often not the hour with the most orders.
cards.use_when: Scheduling campaign sends and deciding whether to trust Klaviyo's Smart Send Time or run your own send-time test.

cards.title: Test content structure in campaigns, not just subject lines
cards.summary: Run campaign content tests (product blocks vs none, bestsellers vs categories) because the learning transfers to flows and future sends, unlike one-off subject line tests.
cards.use_when: Planning campaign experiments and choosing which content variables to vary in your store's promotional and evergreen sends.

cards.title: Use 50/50 manual distribution for email A/B tests
cards.summary: Turn off Klaviyo's automatic distribution and split traffic 50/50 so you keep control of the test and have enough data for a sound winner decision.
cards.use_when: Configuring test settings for subject line or content A/B tests in campaigns and flows.

cards.title: A/B test abandonment flow timing with conditional splits
cards.summary: Test the delay before your abandoned cart and abandoned browse emails by building two flow paths with different wait times, then narrow toward the best delay.
cards.use_when: Optimizing abandoned cart, abandoned checkout, or browse abandonment flow timing to lift placed orders while watching spam complaint rate.

cards.title: Flow subject lines are worth testing, campaign subject lines usually are not
cards.summary: Test subject lines in flows because they run indefinitely, but deprioritize campaign subject-line tests whose results you cannot reuse.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend subject-line testing effort across your welcome, abandonment, and post-purchase flows versus one-time campaigns.

cards.title: Skip CTA-color split tests at small store scale
cards.summary: Button-color A/B tests (yellow vs red) are generally not worth running for stores under roughly $100K/month because the expected lift is too small.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate limited testing capacity for a small or mid-size store's email program, signup forms, or above-the-fold email content.

cards.title: Write email copy that earns attention through value, not cleverness alone
cards.summary: Voice and personality make copy less robotic, but value to the reader is what drives response; build the email around a clear, useful offer first.
cards.use_when: Drafting campaign or flow email copy for product launches, promos, or category sales that need to fit your brand voice.

cards.title: Structure promo emails around headline, code, CTA, products, and closing copy
cards.summary: A tested promotional email layout moves from a clear attention-grabbing headline through an explicit discount code and CTA to recommended products and on-brand closing copy.
cards.use_when: Building the layout and copy order for a discount or category-sale email in your store's campaign calendar.

cards.title: Track place order rate as the primary email KPI hierarchy
cards.summary: Optimize emails for revenue and place order rate first, then click rate, and treat open rate as the least important metric in the chain.
cards.use_when: Choosing the winning metric for any email A/B test or deciding which send-time or content variant to adopt in your store.

cards.title: Sequence send-time tests from wide contrast to narrow pinpointing
cards.summary: Find your best send time by first testing two very different hours, then progressively narrowing around the winner across multiple campaigns.
cards.use_when: Establishing a default campaign send time for your store instead of relying on a single Smart Send Time suggestion.

cards.title: Expect to customize templates to your brand instead of copying them
cards.summary: Templates and flows give you a starting blueprint, but each store must test which retargeting flows, designs, and campaigns its own customers respond to.
cards.use_when: Rolling out a new email program or onboarding templates into your store and setting realistic expectations for iteration.

cards.title: Prioritize money pages over blog content in ecommerce SEO
cards.summary: Prioritize transactional collection and product intent, then assess supporting content by store-specific revenue contribution.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate SEO budget and content effort across collection/product pages versus a blog for a Shopify store.

cards.title: Simplify technical SEO to four essentials
cards.summary: Focus technical SEO only on crawlability/indexing, no broken links, good mobile/desktop UX, and clear page hierarchy.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a technical SEO audit or agency pitch and deciding which fixes are actually worth doing on a store.

cards.title: Evaluate relevant existing-page placements for store referrals
cards.summary: The source prefers existing-page placements; evaluate the relevant audience and cost while qualifying paid links.
cards.use_when: Planning a backlink acquisition campaign or budget and choosing between link insertion and guest posting for a store.

cards.title: Aim for a modest number of quality backlinks, not thousands
cards.summary: For most ecommerce keywords you likely need only 10-20 relevant high-quality backlinks rather than thousands of low-quality ones.
cards.use_when: Setting link-building targets or evaluating a cheap SEO offer that promises large volumes of links.

cards.title: Apply the 80/20 rule to SEO effort and revenue
cards.summary: Roughly 80% of SEO revenue growth comes from 20% of effort: optimizing money pages and acquiring quality backlinks.
cards.use_when: Allocating limited SEO time or budget across reporting, technical fixes, content and link building for a store.
